rejected.title: Presenting a scientific poster
card: A poster communicates an investigation briefly. It has clear sections, such as the aim, method, results, discussion and conclusion, so a reader can follow it quickly.
Use short sentences and labelled graphs, tables and diagrams. Axes and columns need the correct quantity symbols and units, such as v (m s⁻¹).
Report values to a suitable number of significant figures. This should match the precision of the measurements, not every digit on a calculator.
Acknowledge sources, such as books, websites and data from others, in a reference list. This shows which ideas and data are not your own.
rejected.remember: A poster is brief, uses correct symbols, units and significant figures, and credits its sources.

a.q: A student measures a length with a ruler marked in millimetres, and a calculator gives 0.234567 m. What should the poster show?
a.why: The ruler reads to the nearest millimetre, which is 0.001 m, so 0.235 m is suitable. The full calculator value, 0.234567 m, suggests a precision the ruler does not have. Rounding to 0.2 m throws away precision the ruler does give.
a.clue: What is the smallest length the ruler can show, in metres?

b.q: Leila's poster uses a graph from a website and a formula from a textbook. What should she do?
opts: List both sources in a reference list
Leave them out, as they are not her own work
Mention only the textbook, as it is printed
Add the source only if the teacher asks
b.why: Any data, graph or formula that is not her own should be acknowledged. The website and the textbook both count as sources. Leaving them out of the reference list would present others' work as hers.
b.clue: Which of these ideas did Leila not come up with herself?
